Tests of discrimination in searches: hit rates, thresholds, rank order

Source: R/thrtst.R
thrtst.Rd

Asks whether the police search people of one group on less evidence than people of another. Three tests read the same counts of stops, searches and successful searches ("hits", contraband found):

Usage

thrtst(
  stops,
  srch,
  hits,
  grp,
  area = NULL,
  off = NULL,
  ref = NULL,
  level = 0.95,
  maxit = 2000,
  rank = "pair",
  fit = "ml",
  chains = 4,
  iter = 1000,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

stops

The stops of each row: numbers from 0.

srch

The searches among them: numbers from 0, at most stops.

hits

The successful searches: numbers from 0, at most srch.

grp

The group of the people stopped: labels, two groups at least, each with searches.

area

NULL or the area (department, precinct) of each row: labels.

off

NULL or the group of the officers of each row: labels, two groups at least.

ref

The reference group: a label or a position; the first group by default.

level

The confidence level of the intervals: one number strictly between 0 and 1.

maxit

The quasi-Newton steps of each of the three starts of each fit: one whole number from 1.

rank

"pair" or "joint": the rank-order test by pairs of officer groups or for all of them at once.

fit

"ml" or "bayes": the threshold model by maximum likelihood or by Bayesian inference.

chains

The chains of the Bayesian fit: one whole number from 2.

iter

The steps of each chain, half of them warm-up: one whole number from 20.

seed

The seed of the Bayesian fit: NULL to draw it from R's generator, or one whole number from 0.

Value

An object of class thrtst, a list: hit, one row per group (group, stops, srch, hits, srate and hrate, the search and hit rates, and diff, se, z, p of the hit rate against the reference); kpt, the chi-square of equal hit rates (chisq, df, p); thr, one row per group (group, thr, se, lo, hi, and diff, dse, z, p against the reference), NULL when the model is not identified; lrt, the likelihood-ratio test of equal thresholds (stat, df, p, the log-likelihoods llfull and llsame, and the number of cells); fit, one row per model (model, conv, iter; with fit = "bayes" one row with chains, the divergent transitions div, the mean acceptance acc and the step size eps as well); cells, the fitted phi, delta, thr, srate and hrate of each group and area with stops; rank, NULL without off, otherwise with rank = "pair" one row per pair of officer groups and measure (off1, off2, meas, zmin, zmax, rej) and with rank = "joint" one row per measure and officer group (meas, off, rank, rej); ref; and mono, NULL without off, otherwise one row per group of the people stopped and measure (grp, meas, chisq, df, p); post, NULL unless fit = "bayes", otherwise one row per quantity (param, mean, sd, lo, hi, ess, rhat). With fit = "bayes" thr has the columns group, thr, se, lo, hi, diff, dse, dlo and dhi, and lrt is NULL.

Details

  • The outcome (hit-rate) test of Knowles, Persico and Todd (2001): if officers search whenever the chance of finding something is high enough, a group searched on less evidence shows a lower hit rate. The hit rate of each group is compared with the reference group's (difference, Wald standard error, z and two-sided p) and all groups together by Pearson's chi-square of hits and misses among the searched. A hit rate can differ between groups that face the same threshold when their risks are spread differently (the problem of infra-marginality), which the threshold test addresses.

  • The threshold test of Simoiu, Corbett-Davies and Goel (2017), in the fast form of Pierson, Corbett-Davies and Goel (2017). Each stopped person carries a signal, normal with mean delta for those who carry contraband (a share phi of the stopped) and mean 0 for the rest; the officer's estimate of the chance of a hit is the posterior given the signal (a "discriminant distribution"), and a search follows when that chance exceeds the threshold t. In each group and area phi, delta and t are the logistic (phi, t) or exponential (delta) of a group term plus an area term, so a group's threshold may differ from another's by the same amount on the logit scale in every area. With fit = "ml" (the default) the model is fitted by maximum likelihood to the binomial counts of searches among stops and hits among searches. A lower threshold for a group is evidence of discrimination against it. thr is each group's threshold averaged over the areas, weighted by the areas' stops, with a delta-method standard error; the likelihood-ratio test compares the fit with one threshold for every group. The model is fitted only when it has more rates (two per group and area with stops) than parameters (3 (groups + areas - 1)): with area NULL it is not.

  • The tests of Anwar and Fang (2006), when off gives the officer's group. If officers of no group are prejudiced relative to the others, the ranking of the officer groups by search rate is the same for people of every group, and likewise the ranking by hit rate (Proposition 3; Section 2.1.2). mono is their test of monolithic behaviour (Proposition 2, equations 3 and 4; Section 3.2.3): for each group of the people stopped and each measure, Pearson's chi-square of equal rates across the officer groups, on (officer groups - 1) df. With rank = "pair" (the default) each pair of officer groups is taken alone: for each measure the z statistics of the difference across the suspects' groups are given, and rej is TRUE when one is significantly positive and another significantly negative at level (two-sided), a ranking that changes with the suspect's group. With rank = "joint" the ranking of all officer groups is tested at once, as the paper states it: each one-sided z of their equation 7 (the difference of two rates over the root of the sum of the sample variances of the 0/1 outcomes over the counts) beyond the normal quantile at level orders two officer groups among the people of one group; the null of no prejudice holds when one ranking agrees with every such order in every group, and is rejected (rej) when the orders form a cycle (a above b in one group, b above c in another, c above a in a third, or a reversed pair). The common rank (1 the highest rate, ties broken by the pooled rate) is given when it is not rejected. As the paper notes, the test has power below one: a group of officers prejudiced against every group alike is not detected. The paper's p-values come from the normal and chi-square distributions, as here; its resampling (Section 2.2) that balances the officers' assignment across stations needs data on single officers and is not done.

With fit = "bayes" the threshold test is fitted as the papers fit it, by Bayesian inference. The signal distributions are those above, with the area with the most stops as the reference (its terms 0), and each group and area has its own threshold. The priors are those of Simoiu, Corbett-Davies and Goel (2017, Section 2): normal priors with standard deviation 2 on the groups' terms phi_r and delta_r; the areas' terms drawn from N(mu, sigma), with mu ~ N(0, 2) and sigma half normal with scale 2, for each of phi and delta; and each threshold on the logit scale drawn from N(mu_t, sigma_t) of its group, again with mu_t ~ N(0, 2) and half-normal sigma_t. Pierson, Corbett-Davies and Goel (2017) keep this model and put the discriminant distributions in place of the beta distributions of Simoiu et al. The posterior is sampled by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, as both papers do with Stan, here with the No-U-Turn sampler of Hoffman and Gelman (2014) and a diagonal mass matrix: chains chains of iter steps, the first half of each tuning the step size (to an acceptance of 0.8) and the scale of each parameter and then dropped, at most 2^10 leapfrog steps a draw; seed fixes the draws. Each chain starts at the maximum-likelihood fit with every parameter moved at random by up to 0.25, because random starts can leave a chain in a far worse mode. thr then holds each group's threshold averaged over its areas by their stops (posterior mean thr, standard deviation se and the interval lo, hi of probability level) and its difference from the reference group's (diff, dse, dlo, dhi); post gives the same summaries with the effective sample size and the split R-hat of Gelman et al. (2013) for every parameter. The function refuses to report chains that have not mixed: an R-hat of 1.05 or more for any parameter (the rule of Simoiu et al., Section 3.1), or fewer than 100 effective draws of a threshold or a difference; more iterations then help. The data identify the model only when there are more cells with stops than 2 (groups + areas - 1), three groups and five areas at least (Simoiu et al., Section 2); with fewer the function refuses. The authors' published code for the faster model sets other priors (a threshold scale shared by the groups, tighter priors on the areas); the priors here are those the paper states.

The two fits answer under different models and should be reported as such, not as checks of one another. The Bayesian model gives each group and area its own threshold under a hierarchical prior; on data made with one threshold per group (and area offsets) it can report thresholds far from the maximum-likelihood ones and from the values that made the data. For three groups in ten areas with 20,000 stops a cell its posterior means were about 0.13, 0.07 and 0.14, against 0.27, 0.20 and 0.31 from maximum likelihood and from the generating model. Stan's sampler gives the same posterior on the same model, so this is a property of the model, not of the sampler.

Rows are cells of a table (or single stops, with counts of 0 and 1): rows of the same group and area (and officer group) add up.

References

Knowles, J., Persico, N. and Todd, P. (2001). Racial bias in motor vehicle searches: theory and evidence. Journal of Political Economy, 109(1), 203-229. doi:10.1086/318603

Anwar, S. and Fang, H. (2006). An alternative test of racial prejudice in motor vehicle searches: theory and evidence. American Economic Review, 96(1), 127-151. doi:10.1257/000282806776157579

Simoiu, C., Corbett-Davies, S. and Goel, S. (2017). The problem of infra-marginality in outcome tests for discrimination. The Annals of Applied Statistics, 11(3), 1193-1216. doi:10.1214/17-AOAS1058

Pierson, E., Corbett-Davies, S. and Goel, S. (2017). Fast threshold tests for detecting discrimination. arXiv:1702.08536. doi:10.48550/arXiv.1702.08536

Gelman, A., Carlin, J. B., Stern, H. S., Dunson, D. B., Vehtari, A. and Rubin, D. B. (2013). Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed. Chapman and Hall/CRC. doi:10.1201/b16018

Hoffman, M. D. and Gelman, A. (2014). The No-U-Turn sampler: adaptively setting path lengths in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 15, 1593-1623.

Examples

# stops, searches and hits of two groups in four areas
d <- data.frame(
  grp = rep(c("a", "b"), 4), area = rep(1:4, each = 2),
  stops = c(1200, 800, 900, 1100, 1500, 700, 1000, 1000),
  srch = c(60, 70, 50, 95, 80, 66, 52, 90),
  hits = c(24, 18, 19, 25, 30, 17, 21, 24)
)
thrtst(d$stops, d$srch, d$hits, d$grp, area = d$area)
#> thrtst: reference a
#> hit rates (chi-square 10.25 on 1 df, p 0.00137):
#>  group stops srch hits      srate     hrate       diff         se        z
#>      a  4600  242   94 0.05260870 0.3884298  0.0000000         NA       NA
#>      b  3600  321   84 0.08916667 0.2616822 -0.1267475 0.03979326 -3.18515
#>           p
#>          NA
#>  0.00144679
#> thresholds (likelihood ratio 0.03214 on 1 df, p 0.858):
#>  group          thr         se         lo        hi    diff        dse        z
#>      a 0.0001513307 0.09175977 -0.1796945 0.1799972 0.00000         NA       NA
#>      b 0.2601813432 0.02657569  0.2080940 0.3122687 0.26003 0.09569318 2.717331
#>           p
#>          NA
#>  0.00658108
# the rank-order test needs the officers' groups
thrtst(c(100, 100, 100, 100), c(10, 20, 30, 10), c(5, 5, 5, 5),
       grp = c(1, 1, 2, 2), off = c("x", "y", "x", "y"))$rank
#>   off1 off2   meas      zmin     zmax   rej
#> 1    x    y search -2.000000 3.651484  TRUE
#> 2    x    y    hit -1.936492 1.348400 FALSE
# the joint test of three officer groups
thrtst(rep(600, 9), c(72, 48, 60, 60, 72, 48, 48, 60, 72),
       rep(c(36, 24, 30), 3), grp = rep(1:3, each = 3),
       off = rep(c("a", "b", "c"), 3), rank = "joint")$rank
#>     meas off rank   rej
#> 1 search   a   NA  TRUE
#> 2 search   b   NA  TRUE
#> 3 search   c   NA  TRUE
#> 4    hit   a    1 FALSE
#> 5    hit   b    3 FALSE
#> 6    hit   c    2 FALSE
